newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish c.bank ups rates to save current account.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank ups rates to save current account.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland will raise its two main rates on August 4 to curb credit expansion in the economy and put a brake on the fast-growing current account deficit, the central bank's president said on Friday.

Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told a news conference that the bank would raise its lombard rate by two points to 27 percent and its discount rate by 2.5 points to 24.5 percent because earlier efforts to tighten monetary policy bore little fruit.
"The main reason we decided to increase interest rates is because of the continuing fast pace of current account deficit growth in the first half of 1997," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

She said that despite the raising of its market rates since the start of the year and two increases of banks' obligatory reserve requirements, the current account and especially the trade gap had continued to grow too quickly.

"If this pace is sustained for a longer time it may endanger our external trade balance, which would in turn reduce real purchasing power, increase inflation and/or force a socially painful stabilisation process," she said.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said that among other negative trends which fuelled domestic demand, and therefore imports, were the fast growth of real wages and too high a budget deficit.

She said the 2.5 billion zlotys of flood relief credit for the government which parliament imposed on the National Bank of Poland (NBP), was yet another negative factor which led to the interest rate rise.

"The (government flood) credit decision was made too hastily...as (it was) an instrument which could be used at once," she said, adding that in Poland's situation other fiscal instruments, such as a flood tax, would be more appropriate.
Over the last three weeks Poland has suffered its worst flood disaster ever, which killed 54 people, swamped nearly two percent of the country and caused billions of dollars of damage.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said she expected banks to follow the central bank's example and raise their credit rates while not lowering deposit rates.

"To guard against the lowering of deposit rates among banks in response to the central bank rate rise, the NBP will also start collecting six- and nine-month deposits from companies and individuals offering competitive interest," she said.
"We will start collecting the deposits when we are ready."

She added that the government's 13-percent year-on-year inflation target this year against 18.5 percent in 1996 might not be met, but the rate rise would make this year's and next year's single-digit inflation goals more realistic.
"The rate rise is to curb inflation, to come closer to the target, which was not endangered a month ago, but today one can say it is slightly endangered," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.
She said the zloty, recently weakened by the uninspiring current account, is likely to get a boost from the rate rise.
"I would expect the zloty to get a boost, maybe not much, but nevertheless a boost from the interest rate rise, because this is standard market behaviour," she said.

In anticipation of the widely-expected rate rise the zloty rose at Friday's close to -0.8 percent from the trading band centre from about -1.3 percent at opening, but dealers were divided on whether it would make stronger, more sustainable gains.
